inst.force: Ratified by Congress 14 Jan 1784; ratifications exchanged 12 May 1784
inst.prop: Art. 2 sets the boundaries. Arts. 5 and 6 deal with confiscated Loyalist property. Land west of the mountains then came to the United States through the state cessions of 1781 to 1802, which are not shown here.
inst.st: Original states and the land west to the Mississippi, north of 31°

inst.poss: New Orleans 20 Dec 1803; St. Louis 10 Mar 1804
inst.pay: $15 million (60 million francs, plus up to 20 million francs of American claims assumed). BLM gives the cost with interest as $23,213,568.
inst.prop: Art. 3 promises the inhabitants the free enjoyment of their property. Art. 2 passes public lands, buildings and archives. French and Spanish grants became the private land claims of Louisiana, Missouri and Arkansas.
inst.st: LA, AR, MO, IA, OK, KS, NE, most of MN, ND, SD, MT, WY and CO east of the divide

inst.t: West Florida, Mississippi to the Pearl
inst.prop: The United States claimed the district as part of the Louisiana Purchase. Spain gave up its title only in the 1819 treaty. British and Spanish grants here went through the private land claims boards.
inst.st: Louisiana east of the Mississippi (the Florida Parishes)

inst.t: West Florida, Pearl to the Perdido
inst.kind: Act of Congress and occupation (no treaty)
inst.force: Added to Mississippi Territory by act of 14 May 1812
inst.prop: Claimed as part of the Louisiana Purchase; Spain gave up its title only in the 1819 treaty. British and Spanish grants around Mobile and the Gulf coast went through the private land claims boards.
inst.st: Coastal Mississippi and Alabama south of 31°

inst.prop: Art. 2 runs the boundary along the 49th parallel from the Lake of the Woods to the Rocky Mountains. The United States gained the Red River basin south of the line and gave up the part of the Louisiana Purchase north of it. Art. 3 opened the Oregon Country to both nations. BLM lists this ground as "Red River Basin".
inst.st: Red River valley of MN, ND and SD

inst.poss: East Florida 10 Jul 1821; West Florida 17 Jul 1821
inst.pay: No payment to Spain; the United States took on up to $5 million of its citizens' claims against Spain. BLM gives the cost as $6,674,057.
inst.prop: Art. 8 confirms Spanish grants made before 24 January 1818. Art. 3 fixes the boundary along the Sabine, Red and Arkansas rivers and the 42nd parallel; the United States gave up its claim to Texas and Spain its claim to the Oregon Country.
inst.st: FL, and the ground between the 1803 claim and the treaty line in LA and CO

inst.force: Joint resolution 1 Mar 1845; accepted by the Texas convention 4 Jul 1845; admitted as a state 29 Dec 1845
inst.prop: Texas kept its own vacant and unappropriated public lands, so no federal public domain was created inside the state and titles there run from Spain, Mexico, the Republic and the State of Texas. Mexico did not accept the annexation or the Rio Grande boundary until 1848.
inst.st: TX, with Texas's claim to parts of NM, CO, KS, OK and WY

inst.prop: Art. 3 respects the possessory rights of the Hudson's Bay Company and of British subjects; Art. 4 confirms the farms of the Puget's Sound Agricultural Company. Claimed by the United States from the early 1800s and open to both nations from 1818. BLM lists it as "Oregon Compromise".
inst.st: OR, WA, ID, and MT and WY west of the divide

inst.pay: $15 million, plus up to $3.25 million of American claims assumed. BLM gives the cost as $16,295,149.
inst.prop: Arts. 8 and 9 protect the property of Mexicans in the ceded land. Art. 10, on Mexican land grants, was struck out by the Senate. Spanish and Mexican grants were then tried under the California Land Act of 1851, by the surveyors general, and by the Court of Private Land Claims.
inst.st: CA, NV, UT, most of AZ, and parts of NM, CO and WY

inst.kind: Act of Congress, accepted by Texas
inst.force: Act of 9 Sep 1850; accepted by Texas 25 Nov 1850; proclaimed 13 Dec 1850
inst.pay: $10 million in bonds. BLM gives the cost as $15,496,448.
inst.prop: Texas gave up its claim north and west of its present line. Unlike Texas itself, this ground became federal public domain.
inst.st: Parts of NM, CO, KS, OK and WY

inst.prop: Art. 5 carries over the property articles of the 1848 treaty. Art. 6 recognizes only grants that had been located and recorded in the Mexican archives.

Art. 2 passes public lands and buildings and leaves out private individual property; Russian Orthodox churches stay with their congregations. Art. 3 deals with the inhabitants. Very little land was in private title.

inst.kind: Joint resolution of Congress (no ratified treaty)
inst.pay: None; up to $4 million of Hawaiian public debt assumed
inst.prop: The Republic of Hawaii ceded the public, Government and Crown lands. Federal public land laws were not applied; private title runs from the 1848 Mahele (Land Commission Awards and Royal Patents), not from the General Land Office. The Republic followed the 1893 overthrow of the Kingdom, and the annexation is still contested.
Art. 8 says the cession cannot impair private property rights. The same treaty ceded Guam and the Philippines, which are not drawn here.

inst.t: Purchase of the Danish West Indies
inst.prop: Private rights were to be respected. Shown from the signing date, like the rest; the islands changed hands in 1917.

units.label: Louisiana Purchase north of 49°
units.gave: Given up to Great Britain by the Convention of 1818; now in Canada.

units.label: Louisiana Purchase claim in Texas
units.gave: Claim given up to Spain by the 1819 treaty; came back with Texas in 1845.

units.label: Louisiana Purchase claim, later Texas claim
units.gave: Claim given up to Spain by the 1819 treaty; came back with Texas in 1845 and was bought from Texas in 1850.

units.label: Louisiana Purchase claim, later Mexican cession
units.gave: Claim given up to Spain by the 1819 treaty; came back with the Mexican cession in 1848.

source: National Atlas of the United States, Territorial Acquisitions of the United States (usacqup020)
